title: AeroZoo: A Benchmark of Well-Posed Flow Problems for Foundation Models of Aerodynamics
authors: Peter Sharpe, Carmelo Gonzales, Corey Adams, Mehdi Ataei, Sanjay Choudhry
abstract: Neural surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are trained and ranked on datasets that each vary one design family in one flow domain. Such datasets cannot test the least that an aerodynamic foundation model must do: predict CFD-quality incompressible flow in seconds for new shapes in new enclosures. On DrivAerML, larger models and longer training barely lower Transolver's error; doubling the training cases cuts it by about 12% up to 400 cases, exhausting the dataset. We introduce AeroZoo, a benchmark and training corpus of 3,815 time-mean solutions to the unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) equations with a transition model, across seven geometry families, eight enclosure configurations and Reynolds numbers from $10^3$ to $10^8$. Each sample poses a well-posed PDE problem in the form a solver receives it: the boundary meshes grouped by condition type, the prescribed values and the fluid properties. The 2,816 samples with a stable time mean form the canonical benchmark: two tasks, engineering metrics and 22 frozen splits, disjoint in geometry, that hold out geometry families, enclosures, boundary-condition layouts and Reynolds ranges. On the random split, boundary-condition tokens cut GeoTransolver's median velocity error from 76.9% to 8.4% of the inlet speed in single-seed runs (uniform inlet flow: 11.0%). ISLA, a transformer for boundary-driven PDEs, reaches 5.3% over four seeds, about 4 times the change from a finer mesh. On the same test samples, a held-out geometry family barely changes ISLA's error relative to uniform flow, and a held-out enclosure or boundary-condition layout raises it 2.4 to 9.2 times. The data and the scoring code will be released.

infographic.key_insight: AeroZoo shows that boundary-condition inputs are crucial for aerodynamic surrogates, while unseen enclosures and boundary-condition layouts remain harder than unseen geometry families.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable CFD surrogates must generalize across shapes, enclosures and operating conditions—not just predict variations within one design family.
method: Assemble 3,815 time-mean RANS solutions with transition modeling across seven geometry families, eight enclosure configurations and Reynolds numbers from 10³ to 10⁸.
Specify each PDE problem using boundary meshes grouped by condition type, prescribed values and fluid properties.
Evaluate two tasks using engineering metrics and 22 frozen, geometry-disjoint splits.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the random split, boundary-condition tokens reduced GeoTransolver’s median velocity error from 76.9% to 8.4% of inlet speed in single-seed runs; ISLA achieved 5.3% over four seeds.
infographic.watch_item: The canonical benchmark includes only 2,816 samples with stable time means, and held-out enclosures or boundary-condition layouts increased ISLA’s error by 2.4–9.2×.
infographic.paper_title: AeroZoo: A Benchmark of Well-Posed Flow Problems for Foundation Models of Aerodynamics

title: Gradient-Aware AI Agents for Autonomous Turbulence Model Discovery via Differentiable CFD
authors: Yi Liu, Xiantao Fan, Mingqi Xu, Jian-Xun Wang
abstract: Turbulence modeling relies on human choices of closure form, physical inputs, and tunable parameters. Training closures a posteriori is efficient only with gradients through long chaotic rollouts, which few solvers provide. Most a posteriori approaches therefore resort to gradient-free optimization, and nearly all fix the closure form in advance, learning only its parameters. In this work, we introduce a gradient-aware agentic framework that poses closure discovery as a bilevel problem: a multi-agent large language model (LLM) system searches over closure forms, while a GPU-native differentiable computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solver supplies gradients, making differentiable a posteriori learning an action of the autonomous AI agent. For each proposal, the agents construct a differentiable training program by embedding the analytical, neural, or hybrid closure in the solver, implementing a differentiable objective, and validating the gradient path. They then decide whether to evaluate the closure, compute its parameter sensitivities, or train it a posteriori, select the optimization settings, and revise subsequent proposals using the simulation outcomes and returned gradients. Truncated-horizon gradients make this training usable under chaotic dynamics for closures with tens of thousands of parameters. Demonstrations include dissipation-law and subgrid-scale closure discovery in two-dimensional turbulence and wall-model discovery for large-eddy simulation of three-dimensional channel flow. With gradient-based training, the agent recovers reference coefficients that forward evaluation alone does not reach within the same budget, and autonomously discovers and trains analytical and neural closures that improve agreement with the targeted reference statistics. These results demonstrate the feasibility of end-to-end autonomous turbulence model development in time-resolved flows.

infographic.key_insight: Gradient-aware AI agents can autonomously propose, train, and revise turbulence closures by coupling LLM-guided discovery with differentiable CFD.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could reduce manual effort in developing turbulence closures tailored to target flow statistics.
method: Use multi-agent LLMs to search analytical, neural, and hybrid closure forms.
Embed proposals in a GPU-native differentiable CFD solver and validate objectives and gradient paths.
Use simulation results and truncated-horizon gradients to optimize parameters and guide subsequent proposals.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on 2D turbulence and 3D channel-flow LES recovered reference coefficients beyond forward-only evaluation within the same budget and improved agreement with targeted reference statistics.
infographic.watch_item: Transferability beyond the demonstrated flows remains unestablished, and truncated-horizon gradients may miss longer-term effects.
infographic.paper_title: Gradient-Aware AI Agents for Autonomous Turbulence Model Discovery via Differentiable CFD

title: SUMNO: Spatially Unrolled Multigrid Neural Operator for Fluid Flow Surrogates
authors: Yingqi Hu, Nan Deng, Changxiao Shao, Xiaozhou He
abstract: Data-driven surrogate modeling has emerged as a powerful paradigm for accelerating computational fluid dynamics, and hierarchical U-shaped networks, which resemble the structure of classical Geometric Multigrid (GMG) methods, have become prevalent designs. Modern surrogates built on these designs achieve competitive accuracy at a fraction of the cost of numerical solvers; however, accurate prediction of complex flows remains challenging, and no existing architecture leads across them. In such networks, the multigrid analogy mainly concerns the multi-resolution topology, while their components largely follow common vision practice. To address this, this study introduces SUMNO, a multigrid neural operator for fluid flow fields on regular grids that spatially unrolls a V-cycle into a feed-forward U-shaped network. Parameter-free down- and upsampling stand in for restriction and prolongation, and additive skip connections for coarse-grid correction, with normalization-free transfer and skip pathways. Within this macro-architecture, convolutions are used at the fine and intermediate resolutions and shifted-window attention at the coarsest, whose window partitioning is generalized to handle periodicity independently per axis. Evaluated on unseen test configurations across four unsteady and steady flow benchmarks against five representative baselines, SUMNO is best in 5 of 7 settings and ranks second in the remaining two. It reduces the 10-step rollout MSE by about 30% relative to the strongest baseline, and outperforms three baselines with over 130 million parameters using 9.4 million parameters.

infographic.key_insight: SUMNO turns a multigrid V-cycle into a U-shaped neural operator, achieving strong fluid-flow surrogate accuracy with 9.4 million parameters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The architecture offers a parameter-efficient option for predicting steady and unsteady fluid flows on regular grids.
method: Spatially unrolls a V-cycle using parameter-free down/up-sampling and additive skips with normalization-free transfer pathways.
Uses convolutions at fine and intermediate resolutions and shifted-window attention at the coarsest resolution.
Generalizes attention window partitioning to support periodicity independently along each axis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four flow benchmarks and five baselines, SUMNO ranks first in 5 of 7 settings and second in two, reducing 10-step rollout MSE by about 30% versus the strongest baseline.
infographic.watch_item: The reported scope is regular-grid flow fields; applicability to irregular meshes and stability over longer rollouts remain unestablished by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: SUMNO: Spatially Unrolled Multigrid Neural Operator for Fluid Flow Surrogates

title: ISLA: A Coordinate-Free, Measure-Weighted Transformer for Boundary-Driven PDEs
authors: Peter Sharpe
abstract: A foundational principle of physics is that all coordinate systems are equally valid: the behavior of a PDE-governed system does not depend on the origin or orientation of the frame, nor on the units or mesh used to write it down, and neither should a surrogate model. Yet the neural surrogates with the lowest errors on today's aerodynamics benchmarks lack these invariances and fail under simple transformations of the same problem: for models trained on PDEs of cars in one pose (i.e., translation and rotation) and from one mesher, rotating the full PDE raises the surface-pressure error from 4% to more than 100%, and re-sampling its boundary raises it to about 30%. We introduce ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention), a slice-attention transformer for steady, boundary-driven PDEs in which no learned operation receives a coordinate and every sum over the boundary is a quadrature. Positions enter only as distances and relative angles to learned slice anchors, lengths are measured in a unit computed from the boundary, and interior points query the boundary through a tree-accelerated learned kernel without influencing one another. With every boundary cell a token and an exact boundary read, ISLA is equivariant to rigid motions and reflections, invariant to the units of its declared data, and consistent under mesh refinement, while at every setting each query is independent of all other queries. On AeroZoo, 2,816 flows that vary in shape, size, speed, and boundary conditions, its mean reference-scaled velocity and pressure errors are at least 3.1 and 3.3 times lower than any baseline's. On AirfRANS its errors are second only to those of a boundary-integral model (GLOBE) and at least 1.6 times lower than those of Transolver and GeoTransolver.

infographic.key_insight: ISLA builds physical invariances into a transformer for steady, boundary-driven PDEs, making predictions robust to coordinate changes, declared units, and boundary mesh refinement.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach could make aerodynamic surrogates more reliable across object poses, scales, and meshes without retraining for each representation.
method: Uses distances and relative angles to learned slice anchors; no learned operation receives coordinates.
Weights boundary sums by quadrature and normalizes lengths using a boundary-derived unit.
Predicts interior fields through a tree-accelerated learned boundary kernel, with each query independent of other queries.
infographic.evidence_signal: On AeroZoo's 2,816 flows, mean reference-scaled velocity and pressure errors are at least 3.1× and 3.3× lower than any baseline's; on AirfRANS, ISLA ranks behind GLOBE but beats Transolver and GeoTransolver by at least 1.6×.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract evaluates steady, boundary-driven flows; applicability to unsteady turbulence and the cost of exact boundary reads remain to be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: ISLA: A Coordinate-Free, Measure-Weighted Transformer for Boundary-Driven PDEs

title: An Invariant Neural-Network Eddy-Viscosity Closure with Iterative Solver Coupling for Molten Salt Fast Reactor Thermal-Hydraulics
authors: Zaid Abulawi, William Oliveira, Akzhol Almukhametov, Jun Fang, Ling Zou, Rui Hu
abstract: System thermal-hydraulics codes such as the System Analysis Module (SAM) close turbulence on coarse meshes with algebraic zero-equation mixing-length models. These models cannot represent the non-equilibrium turbulence, flow separation, and large-scale recirculation of open-cavity advanced reactors. We develop an invariant neural-network eddy-viscosity closure for SAM and apply it to the Molten Salt Fast Reactor (MSFR). The closure predicts the turbulent kinetic energy and timescale of each element from the flow and geometry of its neighbors, without solving turbulence transport equations. The resulting non-negative eddy viscosity enters the implicit diffusive operator, which keeps the momentum equations well conditioned. We prove that the closure is exactly invariant to translation, Galilean boost, rotation, reflection, and neighbor ordering. A network trained on high-order Nek5000 fields sees a different feature distribution on the coarse SAM mesh. We remove this covariate shift by iteratively retraining the network on SAM flow states against fixed Nek5000 targets. For a held-out steady state, the coupled closure reproduces the single recirculation cell and eddy-viscosity plume of the Nek5000 reference. In a 120 s pump-coastdown transient, it halves the velocity error of the mixing-length model, from 37.6% to 17.7%, and matches the Nek5000 eddy viscosity with a time-averaged relative error of 12%. The remaining velocity error comes from the coarse mesh. The coupled transient takes about 0.2 core-hours, compared with about 330 core-hours for Nek5000. The results show that the closure can recover two-equation RANS turbulence behavior in a coarse-mesh system code at a small fraction of the CFD cost.

infographic.key_insight: An invariant neural-network closure brings two-equation RANS-like turbulence behavior to coarse-mesh reactor simulations without solving turbulence transport equations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The closure improves molten-salt reactor flow predictions at system-code cost, using about 0.2 core-hours versus 330 core-hours for the Nek5000 reference transient.
method: Predict elementwise turbulent kinetic energy and timescale from neighboring flow and geometry.
Enforce translation, Galilean, rotation, reflection, and neighbor-order invariance; place non-negative eddy viscosity in the implicit diffusive operator.
Iteratively retrain on SAM flow states against fixed Nek5000 targets to reduce solver-induced covariate shift.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a held-out steady state, the closure recovered the reference recirculation cell and eddy-viscosity plume; during a 120 s pump coastdown, velocity error fell from 37.6% to 17.7%, with 12% time-averaged eddy-viscosity error.
infographic.watch_item: Coarse-mesh resolution still limits velocity accuracy, and the abstract does not establish generalization beyond the evaluated MSFR conditions.
infographic.paper_title: An Invariant Neural-Network Eddy-Viscosity Closure with Iterative Solver Coupling for Molten Salt Fast Reactor Thermal-Hydraulics

title: Spatiotemporal learning improves quantification of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement
authors: Zhuangzhuang Ma, Rukuan Chai, Qianqian Ma, Yanghua Wang, Branko Bijeljic, Martin J. Blunt
abstract: Pore-space evolution and fluid displacement influence how rocks transmit and store fluids, affecting geological carbon storage, underground hydrogen storage and groundwater contaminant transport. A single time-resolved micro-CT experiment may produce tens to hundreds of three-dimensional images, and segmentation is required to quantify physical properties and run image-based simulations. Traditional methods such as thresholding perform poorly on noisy, low-contrast images and need manual adjustment per image; 3D deep learning networks segment each image without temporal information, so their errors vary between images and could be mistaken for physical change. Here we introduce a transformer-based 4D segmentation framework combining spatial and temporal information. It uses sequential images to resolve ambiguous phase assignments and separate physical change from segmentation error. The method is tested on images of mineral dissolution: it measures pore-volume growth and rock boundaries more accurately than an equivalent 3D model that ignores temporal information. It also captures the increase in permeability verified against reference segmentations and flow simulations. The advantage transfers to another dissolution sample without retraining. On two other datasets of fluid displacement, it reduces spurious changes in predicted rock and porosity fluctuations and accurately identifies filling events. Spatiotemporal segmentation turns sequences of hundreds of three-dimensional images into more reliable quantitative measurements of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement without per-image parameter adjustment to support the analysis of time-resolved CT imaging.

infographic.key_insight: Combining spatial and temporal information improves micro-CT segmentation, helping distinguish real pore-space and fluid changes from segmentation errors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More reliable pore-volume and permeability estimates support analysis of geological carbon storage, underground hydrogen storage and groundwater contaminant transport.
method: Use a transformer-based 4D framework to segment sequential 3D micro-CT images.
Resolve ambiguous phase assignments using spatial and temporal context.
Quantify pore evolution and fluid displacement without per-image parameter adjustment.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on mineral dissolution showed improvements over an equivalent 3D model, with permeability trends verified using reference segmentations and flow simulations; benefits transferred to another dissolution sample without retraining and extended to two fluid-displacement datasets.
infographic.watch_item: Transfer beyond the tested datasets and computational requirements for long 3D image sequences remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Spatiotemporal learning improves quantification of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement

title: Complex nematic dynamics driven by steady Kolmogorov flows
authors: Rahil N Valani, Sumesh P Thampi, Julia M Yeomans
abstract: Complex nematohydrodynamics, including irregular defect dynamics, is commonly associated with time-dependent flows, most notably in active turbulence. Here we consider a simple model of a planar nematic subjected to a temporally steady but spatially varying flow and investigate the onset of time-dependent dynamics. Subjecting a passive nematic to steady Kolmogorov flow, while eliminating velocity fluctuations and hydrodynamic feedback, we find that increasing the flow strength drives a transition from stationary to periodic and, at stronger forcing, irregular spatiotemporal dynamics. The time-dependent states involve repeated local suppression of nematic order and director reorganisation, arising from the competition between spatially varying shear and nematic relaxation. Bifurcation and phase-space analyses characterise this progression, while reduced-order models identify the dynamical origins. A two-mode model captures the onset of periodic motion through a saddle-node infinite-period bifurcation. A five-mode Galerkin truncation further recovers the progression from stationary to periodic and irregular dynamics. These results allow us to explain how a fixed, spatially heterogeneous velocity field can generate temporal complexity through the nonlinear dynamics of nematic order alone.

infographic.key_insight: A steady, spatially varying Kolmogorov flow can drive a passive nematic from stationary to periodic and irregular dynamics without velocity fluctuations or hydrodynamic feedback.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Steady patterned flows could offer a route to controlling time-dependent nematic responses without time-varying forcing.
method: Vary imposed flow strength in a planar passive-nematic model.
Characterise transitions using bifurcation and phase-space analyses.
Use two-mode and five-mode reduced-order models to identify dynamical mechanisms.
infographic.evidence_signal: The two-mode model captures periodic onset through a saddle-node infinite-period bifurcation, while the five-mode Galerkin model recovers stationary, periodic and irregular regimes.
infographic.watch_item: The model excludes velocity fluctuations and nematic feedback on the flow, so applicability to fully coupled systems remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Complex nematic dynamics driven by steady Kolmogorov flows

title: Data-driven Correction Reduced-Order Stochastic Collocation Method for the Time-Dependent Navier-Stokes Equations
authors: Md. Abdul Aziz, Muhammad Mohebujjaman, Xuping Xie
abstract: We develop two hybrid data-driven Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) Reduced-Order Models (ROMs) for the non-stationary incompressible Navier--Stokes Equations (NSEs) with random viscosity. The proposed framework combines Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) ROMs, spatial filtering, data-driven closure modeling, and the Stochastic Collocation Method (SCM). A key feature is the approximation of the realization-dependent closure term by the closure associated with the expected viscosity. Consequently, a single data-driven closure model constructed from the full-order solution corresponding to the expected viscosity can be reused across all realizations, thereby avoiding the expensive construction of realization-specific closure models. This leads to the Data-Driven Correction UQ ROM (DDC-UQ-ROM) and its physically constrained variant, the Constrained DDC-UQ-ROM (CDDC-UQ-ROM), in which physical constraints are imposed on the data-driven correction model. The proposed methods are evaluated for a two-dimensional (2D) flow past a circular cylinder problem with a 5D random viscosity field, considering mean Reynolds numbers $Re=100$ and $Re=500$, different correlation lengths, and both in-sample and out-of-sample parameter settings. Numerical results show that the DDC-UQ-ROM generally improves upon the standard Galerkin ROM (G-ROM), while the CDDC-UQ-ROM exhibits the most accurate and robust approximation of the benchmark energy evolution across the cases considered. The robustness and accuracy of the CDDC-UQ-ROM are further assessed through statistical error analyses of the first- and second-order energy moments, reduced-training-data experiments, and an indicative comparison of wall-clock computational costs with the full-order UQ calculations.

infographic.key_insight: A single data-driven closure trained at the expected viscosity can be reused across random-viscosity realizations, with physical constraints improving reduced-order model accuracy and robustness.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach can reduce the computational burden of uncertainty quantification for unsteady incompressible flows without training a separate closure for every viscosity realization.
method: Combine POD reduced-order modeling, spatial filtering, and stochastic collocation.
Train a shared data-driven correction using the full-order solution at the expected viscosity.
Impose physical constraints in CDDC-UQ-ROM to improve robustness.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on 2D cylinder flow with a 5D random viscosity field at mean Re=100 and 500 covered different correlation lengths and in-sample and out-of-sample settings; CDDC-UQ-ROM best reproduced benchmark energy evolution across the cases considered.
infographic.watch_item: Reusing the expected-viscosity closure is an approximation, and its reliability beyond the tested 2D cylinder-flow regimes remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Data-driven Correction Reduced-Order Stochastic Collocation Method for the Time-Dependent Navier-Stokes Equations

title: Irreversible dynamics for ideal fluids on Riemannian manifolds: metriplectic energy-conserving alternatives to Navier-Stokes
authors: Erwin Luesink, Archishman Saha, Tanya Schmah, Cristina Stoica
abstract: For modelling dissipative phenomena such as friction, diffusion and viscosity, the Hamiltonian framework has a key limitation: once the Casimir invariants are fixed, Hamiltonian flows preserve phase-space volume, which rules out relaxation to equilibrium. Thus modelling dissipation requires modifying the Hamiltonian structure. Following the metriplectic (equivalently, GENERIC) approach, we add to the Hamiltonian vector field a dissipative term generated by a symmetric bracket, here constructed from a Riemannian metric. The resulting flow conserves the energy, and optionally further invariants, while driving a chosen generalised entropy monotonically, which makes the dynamics irreversible; when the entropy is bounded on energy level sets in the direction in which it is driven, it acts as a Lyapunov functional. We apply this construction to ideal fluids on compact Riemannian manifolds, choosing Casimirs of the Lie-Poisson bracket as entropies. In two dimensions, dissipating enstrophy yields the already-known energy-constrained Navier-Stokes equations, which include a nonlocal term restoring energy balance. In three dimensions, where enstrophy is no longer a Casimir, we derive new irreversible models. For incompressible and compressible fluids carrying an advected scalar, dissipating potential enstrophy or higher potential-vorticity moments gives a nonlinear, anisotropic diffusion that acts to align the gradients of the scalar and of the potential vorticity. For a purely incompressible fluid, taking helicity as the entropy gives a first-order, non-smoothing dissipative term whose stationary states are Beltrami fields.

infographic.key_insight: Metriplectic fluid models introduce irreversible dynamics while conserving energy, recovering energy-constrained Navier–Stokes in 2D and yielding new alternatives in 3D.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These models offer a framework for energy-preserving fluid simulation with selective dissipation of quantities such as potential enstrophy or helicity.
method: Augment Hamiltonian fluid dynamics with a symmetric, metric-based dissipative bracket.
Use Casimir invariants as generalized entropies driven monotonically while conserving energy.
Derive scalar-coupled anisotropic diffusion and helicity-driven dynamics on compact Riemannian manifolds.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical model derivations and characterization of stationary states, but no numerical benchmarks or experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: The helicity-driven term is non-smoothing, so monotonic entropy evolution should not be assumed to provide numerical regularization.
infographic.paper_title: Irreversible dynamics for ideal fluids on Riemannian manifolds: metriplectic energy-conserving alternatives to Navier-Stokes

title: Generative AI models for exploring diffusion dynamics from multi-frame particle tracking
authors: Jianan Wei, Qiang Zhang, Hao Sun, Yi Yang, Wenguan Wang
abstract: Particle-based volumetric flow measurement techniques have proven their efficacy in quantitatively assessing the dynamic characteristics of unsteady flows within the realm of fluid mechanics. Despite recent advances in multi-frame particle tracking, an open challenge in this area is maintaining trajectories in temporally under-sampled 3D sequences, where inter-frame displacements are large. In this work, we develop DiffTR-Flow3D, a diffusion-based model that estimates flow motion from spatiotemporal three-dimensional particle recordings via a stochastic diffusion process. DiffTR-Flow3D conditions the diffusion process with both global and local particle dynamics and enhances flow estimation by leveraging historical particle trajectories. Extensive experiments, including numerical simulations and real-world measurements, demonstrate that DiffTR-Flow3D achieves state-of-the-art displacement estimation accuracy compared with learning-based flow estimators, and, when integrated into particle tracking pipelines, substantially improves their long-term tracking performance, while exhibiting robustness and generalization across diverse flow patterns. This work is expected to provide fluid researchers with an effective tool for the consistent and precise analysis of particle trajectories in temporally under-sampled 3D sequences with large inter-frame displacements.

infographic.key_insight: DiffTR-Flow3D uses a conditioned generative diffusion process to estimate 3D particle displacements and improve tracking when large inter-frame motion makes trajectories difficult to maintain.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More reliable particle trajectories can support quantitative analysis of unsteady flows from temporally under-sampled volumetric measurements.
method: Estimate motion from spatiotemporal 3D particle recordings using a stochastic diffusion process.
Condition the model on global and local particle dynamics.
Leverage historical trajectories to improve flow estimation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical simulations and real-world measurements show reported state-of-the-art displacement accuracy versus learning-based flow estimators and improved long-term tracking across diverse flow patterns.
infographic.watch_item: Computational cost and inference latency are not specified in the abstract, leaving deployment feasibility for large particle datasets unclear.
infographic.paper_title: Generative AI models for exploring diffusion dynamics from multi-frame particle tracking

title: Transient CFD simulation of a linear start-up of a variable speed reversible pump-turbine
authors: Aron D. Beck, Alexander Masero, Ernesto Casartelli, Elena Vagnoni
abstract: The integration of intermittent energy sources has led to a growing demand for fast response and partial-load operation of hydraulic turbines, making variable speed units increasingly important. In hydraulic turbines, frequent start-stop cycles generate the highest loads under normal operating conditions. Although historically infrequent and often neglected in turbine design, the growing occurrence of these cycles now necessitates particular consideration due to their contribution to fatigue loading and reduced runner lifetime. Experimental investigations of turbine start-up are costly and cannot be conducted during early design stages. While start-up sequences have been simulated with CFD for fixed speed turbines, each approach has had notable limitations. Some studies have lacked experimental validation. Some studies have used reduced geometrical domains, making it unclear whether inaccuracies stem from geometry simplification or turbulence modelling, and others employ hybrid LES/RANS models, at a very high computational cost, making them unfeasible for use during the design phase. In this study, the linear start-up of a variable-speed turbine start-up is simulated using URANS-based approaches. Simulations are performed using the k-$ω$ SST, EARSM, and the RSM turbulence models within a computationally tractable framework. The simulations show that torque, mass flow, and the blade-passing frequency content at the leading edge are accurately captured by all models. In contrast, the frequency content at the trailing edge and in the draft tube is considerably better resolved using the RSM than the other models because of its capability to consistently capture turbulence anisotropy.

infographic.key_insight: All three URANS turbulence models capture key start-up behavior, but RSM better resolves trailing-edge and draft-tube frequency content by consistently capturing turbulence anisotropy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Computationally tractable start-up simulations can support variable-speed pump-turbine design as frequent start-stop cycles increase fatigue-loading concerns.
method: Simulate a linear start-up of a variable-speed reversible pump-turbine using transient CFD.
Compare k–ω SST, EARSM, and RSM within a URANS framework.
Assess torque, mass flow, and frequency content at blade edges and in the draft tube.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports accurate torque, mass flow, and leading-edge blade-passing frequency content for all models, with substantially better trailing-edge and draft-tube spectral resolution using RSM.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative errors or computational costs, limiting assessment of the accuracy–cost trade-off.
infographic.paper_title: Transient CFD simulation of a linear start-up of a variable speed reversible pump-turbine

title: Harmonic structure and parametric prediction of instantaneous power in oscillating foils
authors: Junjie Shen, Jennifer A. Franck
abstract: A closed-form model is developed to predict the instantaneous lift, pitching moment, and power of an oscillating-foil energy harvester directly from its kinematic input. Such foils extract renewable power from moving water through sinusoidal heaving and pitching. However, due to their large-amplitude motion and vortex-dominated dynamics, classical unsteady aerodynamics cannot accurately predict the time-dependent force and power generation. To generate the model, 405 two-dimensional simulations are computed which vary heave amplitude, pitch amplitude, and frequency, representing the energy harvesting kinematic parameter space. The lift and pitching moment are decomposed into odd Fourier harmonics, and each Fourier coefficient is regressed on sixteen physics-based polynomial terms derived from the kinematic, power, and energy scalings. The regression is performed in two Ridge steps, one for attribution and one for the deployable predictor. The attribution shows that the first harmonic, which contains the mean power, depends on the motion amplitudes. The higher harmonics respond nonlinearly to the frequency, which determines the number and timing of the vortex shedding. The model recovers the cycle-averaged power with a leave-one-out $R^2$ of $0.98$, and reproduces the instantaneous lift with a median peak error of $9\%$ and a median phase error below $1\%$ of the period. The harmonic order of the response counts the discrete vortex events in each stroke, as confirmed by the wake visualization. The model's analytical expression for time-dependent force and power can be utilized as a fast and accurate alternative to high-fidelity simulations, specifically targeting device design and array optimization of oscillating foils.

infographic.key_insight: A closed-form harmonic model predicts oscillating-foil forces and power from motion inputs, linking higher harmonics to discrete vortex-shedding events.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model offers a fast alternative to high-fidelity simulations for renewable-energy foil design and array optimization.
method: Decompose lift and pitching moment into odd Fourier harmonics.
Regress harmonic coefficients on 16 physics-based polynomial terms using two Ridge steps.
Reconstruct instantaneous forces and power from prescribed foil kinematics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 405 two-dimensional simulations, the model achieved leave-one-out R² = 0.98 for cycle-averaged power, 9% median peak error for instantaneous lift, and median phase error below 1% of the period.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to the simulated two-dimensional kinematic parameter space; three-dimensional performance and extrapolation remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Harmonic structure and parametric prediction of instantaneous power in oscillating foils

title: A Conservative Darcy-Brinkman-Stokes Formulation for Digital Rock Flow Simulation with Embedded Second-Brinkman Effects
authors: Gospel E. Stewart, Hannah P. Menke, David Egya, Jacqueline Mifsud, Julien Maes
abstract: Accurate pore-scale direct numerical simulation (DNS) typically requires boundary-conforming meshes on fully resolved geometries, which is memory-intensive and often becomes impractical when modelling complex rock geometries. In contrast, the Darcy-Brinkman-Stokes (DBS) framework enables simulations to be performed directly on voxelized micro-CT images. However, the commonly used simplified DBS formulation (DBS1) neglects the second Brinkman term (SBT) and the porosity-gradient viscous-diffusion term, leading to errors in flow-field characterisation and permeability prediction. Although it is well established that the SBT is essential for capturing viscous boundary effects, it is often assumed that its inclusion requires separate discretisation. In this work, we show that no separate discretisation of the SBT is necessary: writing the DBS equation in its conservative form and applying a standard central differencing scheme in a finite-volume discretisation naturally retains the full DBS formulation. We refer to this formulation as DBS2, and validate its implementation in the GeoChemFoam framework (our open-source computational fluid dynamics simulator based on OpenFOAM) using three benchmark cases: (i) microchannel flow, (ii) a 2D heterogeneous micromodel, and (iii) a 3D micro-CT image of Bentheimer sandstone. Simulation results show that the DBS2 formulation reproduces the DNS velocity field exactly in the microchannel and matches DNS permeability to within 1.5-3.8% in the micromodel and Bentheimer cases at matched spatial resolution. In contrast, DBS1 systematically overpredicts permeability (14.1 to 37.9% in our cases) under the same discretization. Notably, the conservative treatment of the viscous stress preserves the computational efficiency of DBS1 while achieving DNS-level accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: A conservative Darcy-Brinkman-Stokes formulation retains second-Brinkman effects through standard finite-volume central differencing, improving accuracy without separate discretisation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: DBS2 enables accurate digital-rock flow and permeability prediction directly on voxelized micro-CT images while preserving DBS1 computational efficiency.
method: Write the full DBS equation in conservative form.
Apply standard central differencing to retain the full viscous-stress terms.
Implement DBS2 in GeoChemFoam and compare against DNS benchmarks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across microchannel, 2D micromodel, and 3D Bentheimer sandstone benchmarks, DBS2 reproduced the microchannel DNS velocity field exactly and matched DNS permeability within 1.5–3.8% in the latter two cases; DBS1 overpredicted permeability by 14.1–37.9%.
infographic.watch_item: Validation covers three benchmarks at matched spatial resolution; accuracy across broader rock geometries and coarser voxel resolutions remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: A Conservative Darcy-Brinkman-Stokes Formulation for Digital Rock Flow Simulation with Embedded Second-Brinkman Effects

title: Multi-domain AAA-least squares methods and applications
authors: Samuel J. Harris, Ryan A. Palmer
abstract: A multi-domain AAA-least squares (nAAALS) method is developed for computing rational approximations of harmonic functions defined in the interior and exterior of multiply-connected domains. Three classes of problems are considered: i) multi-domain problems where an unbounded exterior is punctured by multiple singly-connected domains; ii) nested domain problems where one domain contains multiple punctured domains; and iii) quasi-steady time-stepping problems where the nAAALS algorithm is coupled with standard Runge-Kutta schemes to compute the coupled evolution of the multiple domain boundaries. The nAAALS method extends the original AAALS algorithm in two key ways. First, a function $\tilde{S}$ satisfying $\tilde{S}(z)=\overline{z}$ on each domain boundary is approximated using the AAA algorithm, producing simple poles distributed according to both the individual boundary geometries and the global multi-domain configuration. Second, the least-squares framework is modified to accommodate the coupled matching conditions across each domain boundary. The method is applied to problems in vortex dynamics to demonstrate its capability, focusing specifically on vortex patches as a working example: finite-area regions of incompressible, inviscid fluid in rotational flow. The nAAALS algorithm is used to (a) reproduce known vortex patch equilibria, and (b) compute the evolution of new and existing non-equilibrium configurations. The results are shown to be accurate at low computational cost, running in seconds on a standard laptop. Crucially, the nAAALS method is suitable for addressing a broader class of steady and quasi-steady multi-domain problems across disciplines, such as those arising in applied mathematics, mathematical biology, and fluid dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: Multi-domain AAA-least squares (nAAALS) efficiently approximates harmonic functions across coupled interior and exterior domains, enabling simulations of interacting vortex patches.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers a low-cost computational approach for coupled boundary problems in inviscid fluid dynamics and potentially other engineering fields.
method: Use AAA rational approximation of boundary conjugate data to place poles according to local geometry and global domain configuration.
Extend least-squares fitting to enforce coupled matching conditions across multiple boundaries.
Couple nAAALS with standard Runge–Kutta schemes to evolve domain boundaries.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports reproduction of known vortex patch equilibria and evolution of equilibrium-displaced configurations, with accurate results computed in seconds on a standard laptop.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantified error or scaling benchmarks, and vortex-patch demonstrations do not establish applicability to general turbulent flows.
infographic.paper_title: Multi-domain AAA-least squares methods and applications

title: Boundary-layer detachment and infinite-Reynolds limit of two-dimensional wall-bounded flows
authors: Ciro S. Campolina, Jérémie Bec
abstract: Understanding boundary-layer detachment and its consequences for the infinite-Reynolds-number limit remains a major challenge in fluid mechanics. Here, direct numerical simulations of incompressible flow in a two-dimensional periodic channel with no-slip walls are used to investigate this problem. Reynolds-number-dependent initial conditions are constructed with a boundary layer of Prandtl thickness that converge in the energy norm to an analytic, stationary Euler flow, while the associated Prandtl system develops a finite-time singularity. Highly resolved simulations show boundary-layer detachment and departures from Prandtl scaling, yet provide numerical evidence that the Navier--Stokes solutions continue to converge to the Euler flow over the simulated time interval. In particular, the squared energy norm of the velocity difference and the time-averaged energy dissipation both scale approximately as $Re^{-1/2}$, consistently with established convergence criteria. Although the detached vortices become more numerous and intense as the Reynolds number increases, their characteristic size and occupied area appear to decrease. These observations suggest how boundary-layer detachment and the breakdown of the Prandtl description can coexist with convergence to a smooth Euler flow.

infographic.key_insight: Boundary-layer detachment and breakdown of Prandtl scaling can coexist with numerical convergence toward a smooth Euler flow as Reynolds number increases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results caution against treating boundary-layer detachment alone as evidence that an inviscid model cannot approximate bulk flow in the energy norm.
method: Run highly resolved direct numerical simulations in a two-dimensional periodic channel with no-slip walls.
Construct Reynolds-dependent initial conditions with Prandtl-thickness boundary layers approaching a stationary analytic Euler flow.
Track velocity-error energy, dissipation, and detached-vortex behavior as Reynolds number increases.
infographic.evidence_signal: Over the simulated time interval, both the squared energy norm of the velocity difference and time-averaged energy dissipation scale approximately as Re^(-1/2), supporting convergence despite detachment.
infographic.watch_item: The evidence is numerical and limited to the studied two-dimensional setup and simulated time interval; it does not establish general or long-time convergence.
infographic.paper_title: Boundary-layer detachment and infinite-Reynolds limit of two-dimensional wall-bounded flows

title: Direct numerical simulation of turbulent heat transfer in water with temperature-dependent viscosity and conductivity
authors: Davide Modesti, Alessandro Ceci
abstract: We study turbulent forced convection of liquid water in a plane channel by direct numerical simulation (DNS), with temperature-dependent viscosity and thermal conductivity. The simulations cover wall heating and cooling, mean-to-wall temperature ratios from 0.83 to 1.3, wall temperatures from 277 to 360\,K and wall Prandtl numbers from 2 to 12. Compared with constant-property flow at the same bulk Reynolds number, the friction coefficient changes by $-39\,\%$ to $+32\,\%$, the heat transfer coefficient referred to the wall Prandtl number changes by up to a factor of $2.3$, and empirical correlations deviate from the DNS by up to $26\,\%$. Instantaneous fields and spectra show that the wall friction Reynolds number misrepresents the range of turbulent scales, whereas near-wall streaks of velocity and temperature have a common spacing when scaled with the local viscous length. The density is constant, so the mean velocity and temperature defects in the core follow those of constant-property flow. To predict friction and heat transfer, we map the mean profiles onto those of constant-property flow through integral transformations derived from the mean momentum and energy balances, with empirical corrections of the eddy viscosity and diffusivity calibrated on the DNS. This approach, developed for air, is extended to liquids, whose conductivity is not proportional to the viscosity and whose Prandtl number varies across the channel. The inverse transformations predict friction and heat transfer within $2\,\%$ of the DNS, except at the lowest Reynolds numbers. The same corrections, introduced in the Spalart--Allmaras model, halve its friction error.

infographic.key_insight: Accounting for temperature-dependent water properties through transformed mean profiles predicts turbulent channel friction and heat transfer within 2% of DNS, except at the lowest Reynolds numbers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach can improve water-cooling and heating calculations where constant-property assumptions misestimate flow resistance and heat transfer.
method: Run direct numerical simulations of heated and cooled water channel flow with temperature-dependent viscosity and conductivity.
Derive integral profile transformations from mean momentum and energy balances, with DNS-calibrated turbulence corrections.
Invert the transformations to predict friction and heat transfer, and test the corrections in the Spalart–Allmaras model.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across wall temperatures of 277–360 K and wall Prandtl numbers of 2–12, friction shifts by −39% to +32% relative to constant-property flow, while empirical correlations deviate from DNS by up to 26%.
infographic.watch_item: Corrections are calibrated on channel-flow DNS; accuracy weakens at the lowest Reynolds numbers, and transfer to other geometries requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: Direct numerical simulation of turbulent heat transfer in water with temperature-dependent viscosity and conductivity

title: Access to the quasi-geostrophic model from within the BK19 compressible flow solver
authors: Amir Maghoul, Rupert Klein
abstract: We extend BK19 the semi-implicit finite-volume solver, to provide access to the quasi-geostrophic (QG) regime within the same compressible framework that already admits soundproof and hydrostatic limits. In order to achieve this goal, we incorporate the asymptotic framework from the continuous theory into the numerical scheme. Adopting the usual asymptotic setting for the quasi-geostrophic regime and using it directly in the numerical model, we perform a scale analysis of the compressible Euler equations in the synoptic length and time scales in the limit of small Rossby number. In this limit, the discrete implicit step recovers geostrophic balance, together with the pseudo-incompressible divergence constraint. We construct a staggered-grid curl operator consistent with the discrete derivatives and use it to define the vorticity in the numerical framework. An asymptotic analysis of the fully discrete scheme then yields a Poisson-type equation for the leading-order Exner-pressure perturbation that coincides with the QG pressure Poisson equation in the continuous theory. As a result of this analysis, we introduce two additional blending switches that (i) convert the elliptic pressure problem from the full Helmholtz to its QG Poisson-type equation and (ii) control whether the horizontal momenta are updated prognostically or diagnosed from geostrophic balance. In combination with the existing soundproof and hydrostatic switches, the resulting algorithm can be operated in fully compressible, pseudo-incompressible, hydrostatic, and QG modes without changing the underlying discretization. The functionality of the numerical scheme in the QG regime is then tested by two idealized vortex test cases to show how stable the vortices remain in the QG run and that, as the Rossby number is reduced, the full compressible scheme converges to slow, balanced QG dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: Extending BK19 with asymptotically derived switches enables quasi-geostrophic dynamics within the same discretization used for compressible, pseudo-incompressible, and hydrostatic flow.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A unified solver can represent fast compressible motion and slow, balanced atmospheric dynamics without switching numerical frameworks.
method: Analyze the fully discrete scheme at synoptic scales in the small-Rossby-number limit.
Construct a consistent staggered-grid curl operator and recover the QG pressure Poisson equation.
Add switches for the pressure equation and prognostic versus geostrophically diagnosed horizontal momenta.
infographic.evidence_signal: Two idealized vortex tests assess QG vortex stability and show convergence of the compressible solver toward balanced QG dynamics as the Rossby number decreases.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to two idealized vortex cases; performance in complex atmospheric flows is not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Access to the quasi-geostrophic model from within the BK19 compressible flow solver

title: A linear stability method based on generalized hydrodynamics: application to high-speed plane Couette flow beyond continuum regime
authors: Zheng Pang, Jihui Ou
abstract: Linear stability analysis of compressible shear flows beyond continuum regime attracts increasing attention in recent years accounting for high-altitude applications. In this paper, the temporal stability of high-speed plane Couette flow in near-continuum regime is addressed. A novel linear stability method based on the generalized hydrodynamic equations (GHE) with slip boundary conditions is developed within the 13-moment framework. Meanwhile, the linear stability equations of the nonlinear coupled constitutive relations (NCCR) and the Navier--Stokes (NS) equations are also given. Based on the developed methods, the linear stability of plane Couette flows at $Ma=2.5$--10 and $Kn=2.7\times 10^{-5}$--0.07 are analyzed, and the rarefaction effects on the base flow, eigenspectrum, mode synchronization and least stable mode are investigated. The results show that the GHE with slip boundary conditions agrees well with direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) results in predicting base flow profiles of velocity, temperature, all stress and heat flux components, while the NS equations show considerable differences, especially for capturing the nonlinear normal stress and tangential heat flux. The GHE-based linear stability theory (LST) recovers to the classical NS-based LST in the continuum limit, while they show considerable differences when $Kn$ reaches $O(0.01)$. As rarefaction degree increases, the synchronization between acoustic modes and viscous modes becomes weak, and all modes become stable in rarefied plane Couette flow. The surface slip effect and nonlinear transport increase the disturbance phase speeds, while they have different effects on the growth rate of different modes. Generally, rarefaction effects increase the growth rate of the least stable Mode II at low wavenumbers, and show more pronounced effects on higher modes and high-wavenumber disturbances.

infographic.key_insight: Generalized hydrodynamic stability analysis captures rarefaction effects missed by Navier–Stokes theory, revealing weaker acoustic–viscous mode synchronization and eventual stabilization of all modes as rarefaction increases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports stability assessment of high-speed, low-density shear flows relevant to high-altitude aerospace applications.
method: Develop temporal linear stability analysis using 13-moment generalized hydrodynamic equations with slip boundary conditions.
Compare predictions with nonlinear coupled constitutive relations and Navier–Stokes formulations.
Examine base flows, eigenspectra, mode synchronization, and disturbance growth across Mach and Knudsen numbers.
infographic.evidence_signal: For Ma = 2.5–10 and Kn = 2.7×10⁻⁵–0.07, generalized hydrodynamic base-flow predictions agree well with DSMC, while stability predictions differ considerably from Navier–Stokes results near Kn = 0.01.
infographic.watch_item: DSMC agreement is reported for base-flow profiles; it should not be interpreted as direct validation of disturbance growth rates or extrapolated beyond the studied near-continuum regime.
infographic.paper_title: A linear stability method based on generalized hydrodynamics: application to high-speed plane Couette flow beyond continuum regime

title: A thermodynamically consistent, fully compressible, fluctuating hydrodynamics model of a Cahn Hilliard binary fluid mixture
authors: Anuj Chaudhri
abstract: We derive, from first principles, a thermodynamically consistent set of fully compressible fluctuating hydrodynamic equations for a Cahn-Hilliard binary fluid mixture, in isothermal and non-isothermal form and for symmetric and non-symmetric mixtures. The derivation uses the GENERIC formalism, with the friction operator constructed from flux fluctuations following Jelic and Ottinger, so that deterministic and stochastic fluxes derive from the same operator and correlation matrix and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem holds by construction. We show that the momentum equation must use the total mass density, that the Cahn-Hilliard variable is the mass fraction, and that the diffusion flux must be driven by the specific, not the volumetric, exchange potential. We derive a generalized Korteweg tensor for square-gradient energies in density and composition, and show that the reversible pressure tensor of the non-isothermal model is fixed by the degeneracy condition, producing a thermal capillary stress when the interfacial free energy has an entropic part. Thermodynamic consistency is proved in full: Jacobi identity, positivity and degeneracy, local energy conservation with interstitial-working fluxes, a local entropy balance, Soret-Dufour reciprocity, and Einstein statistics of the linearized equations. The final equations are written in conservative form for finite-volume discretization, and closed-form static and dynamic structure factors are given for all models as analytic benchmarks. An appendix shows that the same models follow from classical irreversible thermodynamics with the Helmholtz or Gibbs free energy; this route is unique for isothermal flows and has a gauge freedom in the non-isothermal case that GENERIC removes.

infographic.key_insight: A first-principles model unifies fully compressible Cahn–Hilliard mixture dynamics with thermal fluctuations while enforcing thermodynamic consistency and fluctuation–dissipation balance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Conservative equations and analytic structure factors provide a foundation for finite-volume simulations and verification of fluctuating binary-fluid solvers.
method: Use GENERIC to derive deterministic and stochastic fluxes from a shared friction operator.
Evolve total mass density and composition mass fraction, with diffusion driven by the specific exchange potential.
Derive generalized Korteweg stresses for isothermal and non-isothermal, symmetric and non-symmetric mixtures.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical consistency proofs and closed-form static and dynamic structure factors as benchmarks, rather than numerical or experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: A discretized solver must preserve the continuum model’s conservation laws and fluctuation–dissipation balance; conservative form alone does not guarantee this.
infographic.paper_title: A thermodynamically consistent, fully compressible, fluctuating hydrodynamics model of a Cahn Hilliard binary fluid mixture

title: Rotationally Symmetric Lattice Boltzmann Pseudopotential Methods for Porous Media Applications
authors: Benjamin Kellers, Arnulf Latz, Timo Danner
abstract: Pseudopotential models are a well established approach for multiphase and multicomponent simulations using the lattice Boltzmann method. Although not the most accurate, they are often chosen for ease of implementation and adaptability. A drawback of the models are spurious currents at the interfaces and particularly at solid walls which introduce numerical artifacts. An improved lattice Boltzmann pseudopotential model is presented. The discrete fluid density gradients in the coupling force are computed with rotationally symmetric gradient operators formulated as a convolution. As a result, spurious currents are reduced in settings where solid walls are unaligned with the lattice directions. Additionally, variations of introducing fluid-solid interaction either equally through both fluids or through a single fluid only are compared. Presented model variants are compared using droplets on walls as a common benchmark, analytically solvable capillary rise experiments (Jurin's law), and porous media imbibition as a practical application. Rotationally symmetric operators outperform the classical lattice weights approach in all tests in terms of accuracy, while avoiding extending the lattice to compute higher order gradients. The choice of the fluid-solid interaction variant depends on the problem under consideration and the desired properties of the resulting model.

infographic.key_insight: Rotationally symmetric gradient operators improve pseudopotential lattice Boltzmann accuracy and reduce spurious currents near solid walls unaligned with the lattice.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports more accurate multiphase simulations of capillary transport and porous-media imbibition without extending the lattice for higher-order gradients.
method: Compute coupling-force density gradients using rotationally symmetric convolution operators.
Compare fluid–solid interactions applied through both fluids versus a single fluid.
Benchmark against the classical lattice-weights approach.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved accuracy across wall-droplet benchmarks, capillary rise evaluated against Jurin’s law, and porous-media imbibition tests.
infographic.watch_item: The preferred fluid–solid interaction variant remains problem-dependent; the abstract provides no quantitative error reductions.
infographic.paper_title: Rotationally Symmetric Lattice Boltzmann Pseudopotential Methods for Porous Media Applications
